claim: The inner ear is a fluid-filled closed-epithelial structure whose function requires maintenance of an internal hydrostatic pressure and fluid composition.
source: The inner ear is a fluid-filled closed-epithelial structure whose function requires maintenance of an internal hydrostatic pressure and fluid composition.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about inner ear physiology that draws from established scientific knowledge about inner ear function.

claim: The endolymphatic sac (ES) is a dead-end epithelial tube connected to the inner ear whose function is unclear.
source: The endolymphatic sac (ES) is a dead-end epithelial tube connected to the inner ear whose function is unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges the anatomical structure of the ES and the lack of clarity about its function prior to this study.

claim: ES defects can cause distended ear tissue, a pathology often seen in hearing and balance disorders.
source: ES defects can cause distended ear tissue, a pathology often seen in hearing and balance disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about ES pathology in hearing and balance disorders.

claim: The ES undergoes cycles of slow pressure-driven inflation followed by rapid deflation.
source: Using live imaging of zebrafish larvae, we reveal that the ES undergoes cycles of slow pressure-driven inflation followed by rapid deflation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by live imaging data presented in Figures 1D-G and Videos 2-3.

claim: Absence of ES inflation-deflation cycles in lmx1bb mutants leads to distended ear tissue.
source: Absence of these cycles in lmx1bb mutants leads to distended ear tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lmx1bb mutant analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ES contains a pressure relief valve comprised of partially separated apical junctions and dynamic overlapping basal lamellae that separate under pressure to release fluid.
source: Using serial-section electron microscopy and adaptive optics lattice light-sheet microscopy, we find a pressure relief valve in the ES comprised of partially separated apical junctions and dynamic overlapping basal lamellae that separate under pressure to release fluid.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data (Figure 4) and AO-LLSM data (Figures 5-7).

claim: This lmx1-dependent pressure relief valve is required to maintain fluid homeostasis in the inner ear and other fluid-filled cavities.
source: We propose that this lmx1-dependent pressure relief valve is required to maintain fluid homeostasis in the inner ear and other fluid-filled cavities.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings with lmx1bb mutants and the observed valve structure.

claim: Hydrostatic pressure inflates the eye during development.
source: Hydrostatic pressure inflates the eye during development (Coulombre, 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Unstable ocular pressure from reduced production of aqueous humor or reduced drainage can lead to blindness, as occurs in hypertonic maculopathy or glaucoma.
source: Later, unstable ocular pressure from reduced production of aqueous humor or reduced drainage can lead to blindness, as occurs in hypertonic maculopathy or glaucoma (Costa and Arcieri, 2007; Leske, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ocular pressure and disease.

claim: Hydrostatic pressure appears to drive expansion of brain ventricles during development.
source: Hydrostatic pressure appears to drive expansion of brain ventricles during development (Desmond, 1985; Desmond and Levitan, 2002; Lowery and Sive, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on brain ventricle development.

claim: Unstable hydrostatic pressure in brain ventricles is correlated with hydrocephaly and mental disorders.
source: Later, unstable hydrostatic pressure in brain ventricles is correlated with hydrocephaly and mental disorders (Hardan et al., 2001; Kurokawa et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on brain ventricle pathology.

claim: Hydrostatic pressure inflates and controls the size of the developing ear.
source: Hydrostatic pressure inflates and controls the size of the developing ear (Abbas and Whitfield, 2009; Hoijman et al., 2015; Mosaliganti et al., unpublished).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and unpublished data.

claim: Unstable pressure in the ear can cause deafness and balance disorders like Pendred syndrome and Ménière's disease.
source: Later, unstable pressure in the ear can cause deafness and balance disorders like Pendred syndrome and Ménière's disease (Belal and Antunez, 1980; Schuknecht and Gulya, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ear pathology.

claim: Tissue structures identified as important for pressure control include Schlemm's canal in the eye, arachnoid granules and the choroid plexus in the brain, and the endolymphatic duct and sac in the ear.
source: Tissue structures identified as important for pressure control include Schlemm's canal in the eye, arachnoid granules and the choroid plexus in the brain, and the endolymphatic duct and sac in the ear (Johnstone et al., 2011; Kimura and Schuknecht, 1965; Naito, 1950; Orešković et al., 2017; Pollay, 2010; Symss and Oi, 2013; Tripathi, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on pressure control structures.

claim: The inner ear is filled with endolymph, the composition of which differs from other fluids such as plasma, perilymph, and cerebral spinal fluid in that it contains high potassium, low sodium, and high electric potential.
source: It is filled with endolymph, the composition of which differs from other fluids such as plasma, perilymph, and cerebral spinal fluid in that it contains high potassium, low sodium, and high electric potential (Lang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on endolymph composition.

claim: This endolymph composition is necessary to drive ion currents into hair cells to convert fluid movement, caused by either the head's acceleration or by sound, into biochemical signals that underlie balance and hearing.
source: This endolymph composition is necessary to drive ion currents into hair cells to convert fluid movement, caused by either the head's acceleration or by sound, into biochemical signals that underlie balance and hearing.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about inner ear function and hair cell physiology.

claim: An ES-like structure is present in basal vertebrates, including lamprey and hagfish, suggesting it plays an ancient role in inner ear function.
source: An ES-like structure is present in basal vertebrates, including lamprey and hagfish (Hammond and Whitfield, 2006), suggesting it plays an ancient role in inner ear function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and includes an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claim: The epithelium of the ES, as well as that of the rest of the ear, has an apical surface facing the internal endolymph and a basal surface facing the external perilymph.
source: The epithelium of the ES, as well as that of the rest of the ear, has an apical surface facing the internal endolymph and a basal surface facing the external perilymph (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the illustration in Figure 1A and established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Most of the adult ear is enclosed in a bony labyrinth within the temporal bone and perilymph is located in the space between the epithelium and bone.
source: Most of the adult ear is enclosed in a bony labyrinth within the temporal bone and perilymph is located in the space between the epithelium and bone (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the illustration in Figure 1A and established anatomical knowledge.

claim: In adults, the endolymphatic duct and sac are partially encased within the temporal bone such that the distal end of the endolymphatic sac protrudes out of the temporal bone into the cranial cavity.
source: In adults, the endolymphatic duct and sac are partially encased within the temporal bone such that the distal end of the endolymphatic sac protrudes out of the temporal bone into the cranial cavity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the illustration in Figure 1A and established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Excessive hydrostatic pressure can tear the inner ear's epithelium, disrupting its electric potential (a pathology called endolymphatic hydrops).
source: Excessive hydrostatic pressure can tear the inner ear's epithelium, disrupting its electric potential (a pathology called endolymphatic hydrops).
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about inner ear pathology.

claim: Low potassium or reduced endolymph production can lower hydrostatic pressure within the ear to the point where the ear chambers may collapse.
source: In contrast, low potassium or reduced endolymph production can lower hydrostatic pressure within the ear to the point where the ear chambers may collapse (Lang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Early work showed that ES ablation causes hydrostatic pressure to rise and the epithelium to tear, suggesting that the ES may maintain endolymph homeostasis.
source: Early work showed that ES ablation causes hydrostatic pressure to rise and the epithelium to tear (Kimura and Schuknecht, 1965; Naito, 1950), suggesting that the ES may maintain endolymph homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and includes an inference about ES function.

claim: Recent work indicated that an explanted mouse ES gradually loses endolymph.
source: Recent work indicated that an explanted mouse ES gradually loses endolymph (Honda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: While many molecular pores and transporters are expressed in the ES, it is unclear why it is organized as a dead-end tube and how it might reduce endolymph volume.
source: While many molecular pores and transporters are expressed in the ES, it is unclear why it is organized as a dead-end tube and how it might reduce endolymph volume.
evidence: This statement acknowledges existing knowledge about ES molecular components while highlighting gaps in understanding.

claim: ES morphogenesis begins at 36 hr post fertilization (hpf) as an evagination in the dorsal epithelial wall of the otic vesicle.
source: We saw that ES morphogenesis begins at 36 hpf as an evagination in the dorsal epithelial wall of the otic vesicle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1, Figure 1A–B, and ES identity confirmed by expression of foxi1, Figure 1B').
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1, and confirmed by foxi1 expression in Figure 1B'.

claim: Between 36 and 60 hpf, the ES grows and elongates.
source: Between 36 and 60 hpf, the ES grows and elongates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-lapse imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The zebrafish ear starts to sense body acceleration for the nervous system between 60 and 72 hpf, as demonstrated by the onset of the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
source: The zebrafish ear starts to sense body acceleration for the nervous system between 60 and 72 hpf, as demonstrated by the onset of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (Mo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ES begins to exhibit a physical behavior during the same time window (60-72 hpf).
source: We found that the ES begins to exhibit a physical behavior during the same time window.
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data presented in Figures 1D-G.

claim: The lumen of the ES remains closed until 60 hpf, but between 60 and 65 hpf it begins cycles of slowly inflating and rapidly deflating.
source: We observed that the lumen of the ES remains closed until 60 hpf, but between 60 and 65 hpf it begins cycles of slowly inflating and rapidly deflating (sagittal slices, Figure 1D, lumen volumes, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Videos 2–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 1D-E and Videos 2-3.

claim: The ES lumen volume changes 5–20-fold through the course of each cycle.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) measurements showed that the ES lumen volume changes 5–20-fold through the course of each cycle (Figure 1E,F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 1E-F.

claim: The period between peak ES volumes exhibited a broad distribution (0.3–4.5 hr) with an average of 1.6 ± 0.8 hr.
source: The period between peak ES volumes exhibited a broad distribution (0.3–4.5 hr) with an average of 1.6 ± 0.8 hr (mean ± SD, histogram compiled from eight time courses and 54 peaks, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of multiple time courses shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The duct is open and endolymph flows from the otic vesicle into the ES during inflation.
source: We found that the duct is open and that endolymph flows from the otic vesicle into the ES during inflation (Figure 2A–D, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by dye injection experiments shown in Figure 2A-D and Video 4.

claim: Upon deflation, endolymph rapidly leaked out of the ES and into the perilymphatic space.
source: Additionally, upon deflation, endolymph rapidly leaked out of the ES and into the perilymphatic space (75:22 panel, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Laser ablation of 2–3 cells within the wall of the otic vesicle distant from the ES at 64 hpf causes the ES to deflate and completely collapse within 20 min.
source: To determine whether pressure in the otic vesicle is transmitted to the ES for its inflation, we laser-ablated 2–3 cells within the wall of the otic vesicle distant from the ES at 64 hpf (Figure 2E). Shortly after ablation, the ES deflated and completely collapsed within 20 min (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume.
source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: The ES tissue has elastic material properties.
source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rapid collapse of the ES after laser ablation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
source: These results indicate that fluid pressure in the otic vesicle inflates the ES volume, the ES tissue has elastic material properties, and a loss of epithelial integrity is sufficient for ES deflation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the laser ablation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Perilymph dye begins to leak into the ES lumen at the onset of each deflation.
source: Quantification of fluorescence within the lumen of the ES revealed that perilymph dye begins to leak into the ES lumen at the onset of each deflation (Figure 1F, visible leakage in Figure 1D, Videos 2–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1F and imaging data in Figure 1D and Videos 2-3.

claim: Deflation coincided with an influx of fluorescence from the perilymph into the lumen of the ES in each of the nine major inflation-deflation cycles.
source: In the example shown deflation coincided with an influx of fluorescence from the perilymph into the lumen of the ES in each of the nine major inflation-deflation cycles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Both deflation and dye leakage were due to transient breaks in the epithelial barrier.
source: This coincident timing suggests that both deflation and dye leakage were due to transient breaks in the epithelial barrier, an interpretation that is consistent with the rapid release of endolymph prior to deflation (Figure 2D, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the coincident timing of deflation and dye leakage shown in Figures 1F and 2D.

claim: Endolymph efflux occurs at the same time as perilymph influx during deflation.
source: To determine whether endolymph efflux occurs at the same time as perilymph influx, we simultaneously labeled the two fluids with different colored dyes and imaged their localization with higher temporal resolution (Figure 2G, Video 5). We found a fluttering behavior underlying deflation in which endolymph leaked out (62:41:20), perilymph leaked in (62:55:20), leaked-in perilymph flushed out with more endolymph efflux (62:55:40), followed by complete deflation (63:12:00).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual-dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 2G and Video 5.

claim: A plausible mechanism for the observed behavior involves a structure that normally resists flow driven by a pressure differential that rapidly opens during deflation to allow for fast efflux by advection followed by influx by diffusion before re-closing.
source: A plausible mechanism for this observed behavior involves a structure that normally resists flow driven by a pressure differential that rapidly opens during deflation to allow for fast efflux by advection followed by influx by diffusion before re-closing.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed fluttering behavior during deflation.

claim: The ES in lmx1bb mutants became greatly enlarged (>4 times the inflated wild-type ES volume) making it readily visible at 80 hpf by bright-field microscopy.
source: We found that the ES in lmx1bb mutants became greatly enlarged (>4 times the inflated wild-type ES volume) making it readily visible at 80 hpf by bright-field microscopy (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The lmx1bb reporter (Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP)mw10) was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation.
source: This reporter was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation (cyan, Figure 3B), consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of the lmx1bb reporter shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lmx1bb reporter expression is consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
source: This reporter was expressed in ES cells beginning at 52–58 hpf, just before the first ES inflation (cyan, Figure 3B), consistent with lmx1bb expression being instrumental for development of the ability of the ES to release pressure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of lmx1bb reporter expression relative to ES inflation cycles.

claim: Earlier in the development of the otic vesicle, lmx1bb is expressed in portions of the nascent semicircular canals and sensory patches, regions of the inner ear that also exhibit abnormal development in the mutant.
source: Earlier in the development of the otic vesicle, lmx1bb is expressed in portions of the nascent semicircular canals and sensory patches, regions of the inner ear that also exhibit abnormal development in the mutant (Obholzer et al., 2012; Schibler and Malicki, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on lmx1bb expression and mutant phenotypes.

claim: There is no precedent for ES development being dependent on those portions of the otic vesicles and there are many mutants with similar SCC or sensory defects that do not have ES phenotypes.
source: There is no precedent for ES development being dependent on those portions of the otic vesicles and there are many mutants with similar SCC or sensory defects that do not have ES phenotypes (Fekete, 1999; Malicki et al., 1996; Whitfield et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on inner ear mutants.

claim: The ES lumen over-inflates in lmx1bbjj410/jj410 mutant embryos.
source: Live imaging and perilymph tracking in lmx1bbjj410/jj410 mutant embryos revealed that the ES lumen over-inflates (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Videos 6–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 3C-D and Videos 6-7.

claim: In the lmx1bb mutant, perilymph was never observed entering the ES.
source: In the mutant, however, we never observed perilymph entering the ES.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Endolymph leakage out of the distended ES epithelium was not observed in mutants where the endolymph was labeled.
source: Additionally, we imaged mutants where the endolymph was labeled and did not observe leakage out of the distended ES epithelium (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The epithelial diffusion barrier remains intact in the mutant ES.
source: These findings suggest that the epithelial diffusion barrier remains intact in the mutant ES.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of perilymph entry and endolymph leakage in the mutant ES.

claim: The ES tissue was much thinner in wild-type embryos during peak inflation than in the corresponding region in mutants inflated to a similar volume.
source: Indeed, by comparing the dorsal ES tissue between wild-type and lmx1bb mutants using confocal microscopy and membrane-localized fluorescent proteins, we observed that the ES tissue was much thinner in wild-type embryos during peak inflation than in the corresponding region in mutants inflated to a similar volume (thin region indicated by asterisk, Figure 3F,G, data in G compiled from 65 to 80 hpf inflation events).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3F-G.

claim: In wild-type embryos, the thin region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm).
source: In wild-type embryos, this region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm, the mutant, n = 9, is significantly thicker than wild-type, n = 14, with a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The mutant ES is significantly thicker than wild-type (Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
source: In wild-type embryos, this region often appeared as a thin sheet (1.0 ± 0.3 µm, mean ±SD) rather than thick as seen in the un-inflated wild-type ES or the lmx1bb mutants in which two distinct surfaces (apical and basal) were observed (6.2 ± 3.2 µm, the mutant, n = 9, is significantly thicker than wild-type, n = 14, with a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon one tailed p-value of 4 × 10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of thickness measurements.

claim: Imaging the uneven signal of the Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP) reporter revealed thin protrusions that extend along the basal side of neighboring ES cells.
source: Imaging the uneven signal of the Tg(lmx1bb:eGFP) reporter revealed thin protrusions that extend along the basal side of neighboring ES cells (white arrow, Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Sparse mosaic labeling of cells in the wild-type confirmed the presence of thin basal protrusions in the ES, as well as diversity in their organization.
source: Sparse mosaic labeling of cells in the wild-type further confirmed the presence of thin basal protrusions in the ES, as well as diversity in their organization (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Similar labeling in the mutant revealed the absence of thin basal protrusions in the ES.
source: Similar labeling in the mutant revealed the absence of thin basal protrusions in the ES (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The basal surface of the ES tissue faces the perilymph outside surrounding the otic vesicle.
source: We found that the basal surface of the ES tissue faces the perilymph outside surrounding the otic vesicle (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: A clear difference in the staining pattern of collagen between wild-type and the lmx1bb410/410 mutant could not be resolved.
source: We could not resolve a clear difference in the staining pattern of collagen between wild-type and the lmx1bb410/410 mutant.
evidence: This is a negative result from immunostaining experiments.

claim: Prior work suggested that Col1a2 may be a direct target of LMX1B in the limb.
source: Prior work suggested that Col1a2 may be a direct target of LMX1B in the limb (Haro et al., 2017) and additional studies will be necessary to determine whether collagen or other extracellular matrix components are abnormally expressed in the ES of lmx1bb410/410 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ZO-1 stained the ES tissue that faces the endolymph-filled lumen.
source: We also examined localization of the apical marker ZO-1 and found that it stained the ES tissue that faces the endolymph-filled lumen (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3K-L.

claim: This apical-basal organization was also present in the lmx1bb410/410 mutant.
source: This apical-basal organization was also present in the lmx1bb410/410 mutant (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3K-L.

claim: The absence of local breaks in the mutant ES, the absence of regional thinning in the mutant inflated ES, and the absence of thin basal protrusions suggests that these thin areas may be structurally relevant to ES pressure relief.
source: The absence of local breaks in the mutant ES, the absence of regional thinning in the mutant inflated ES, and the absence of thin basal protrusions suggests that these thin areas may be structurally relevant to ES pressure relief.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and mutant ES structures.

claim: The dorsal tissue of the inflated wild-type sac consists of an extremely thin shell of broadly overlapping lamellae extending from the basal sides of multiple adjacent cells.
source: We found the dorsal tissue of the inflated wild-type sac consists of an extremely thin shell of broadly overlapping lamellae extending from the basal sides of multiple adjacent cells (Figure 4; Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4 and Video 8.

claim: These basal extensions appear to be the distal barrier in the ES because the endolymph they contain is continuous with the lumen of the ES and endolymphatic duct.
source: These basal extensions appear to be the distal barrier in the ES because the endolymph they contain is continuous with the lumen of the ES and endolymphatic duct (extending ventrally from outlined ES lumen in third panel of Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the EM data showing continuity of the endolymph space.

claim: Lamellar sheets extend for distances as long as a typical cell body but are as thin as 40 nm.
source: We observed lamellar sheets that extend for distances as long as a typical cell body but are as thin as 40 nm (Figure 4A,F; lamella from cell segmented in purple extends 7.5 μm in the x-y plane and 6.6 μm along the z-axis).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4A and 4F.

claim: The lamellae from ES cells formed large zones of overlap and sometimes bifurcated to form a tongue-and-groove structure or interwoven structures.
source: In contrast to junctions between thin aveolar cells, which kiss at their tips with tight junctions, the lamellae from ES cells formed large zones of overlap and sometimes bifurcated to form a tongue-and-groove structure (Figure 4B, inset) or interwoven structures (Figure 4C,F, black mesh highlights area of overlap, dotted perimeter indicates full spread).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4B-C and 4F.

claim: These structures lacked electron-dense signal, indicating that they were unlikely to contain tight junctions between lamellae.
source: These structures lacked electron-dense signal, indicating that they were unlikely to contain tight junctions between lamellae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of electron-dense signal in the EM data.

claim: An ear was identified where the lamellar barriers were separated as if forced into an open configuration.
source: We also identified an ear where the lamellar barriers were separated as if forced into an open configuration (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: This may be an ES in the act of deflating via bursting or sliding of the lamellae.
source: This may be an ES in the act of deflating via bursting or sliding of the lamellae.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EM data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The full serial-section EM dataset confirmed that the endolymphatic duct connects the lumen of the otic vesicle to the tip of the ES, where basal lamellae form a complete barrier.
source: The full serial-section EM dataset also confirmed that the endolymphatic duct connects the lumen of the otic vesicle to the tip of the ES, where basal lamellae form a complete barrier (available at http://zebrafish.link/hildebrand16, ES-specific links presented in methods) (Hildebrand et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the full serial-section EM dataset referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Basal lamellae were present along the length of the endolymphatic duct.
source: Basal lamellae were present along the length of the endolymphatic duct.
evidence: This claim is supported by the serial-section EM data.

claim: Cell bodies in the duct remain tightly packed with apical junctions unlike the apical and lateral membrane separations exposing lamellae in the ES.
source: However, cell bodies in the duct remain tightly packed with apical junctions (Figure 4A,E) unlike the apical and lateral membrane separations exposing lamellae in the ES.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4A and 4E.

claim: Electron-dense tight junctions are present in cells that also have spread basal protrusions.
source: We identified electron-dense tight junctions between cells at the tip of the ES. These same cells also had lamellar projections (yellow arrows indicate tight junctions, Figures 4G and 3 serial EM sections, 1.2 μm apart, the diameter of the apical opening is ~1.2 μm).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The electron-dense signal formed a ring sealing the apical side of these ES cells that was continuous except for an opening that connected fluid from the duct and sac to the exposed lamellae.
source: The electron-dense signal formed a ring sealing the apical side of these ES cells that was continuous except for an opening that connected fluid from the duct and sac to the exposed lamellae (magenta arrow directed from duct to sac, Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Apical junctions were also present in the mutant ES of lmx1bbjj410/jj410 larvae.
source: Apical junctions were also present in the mutant ES of lmx1bbjj410/jj410 larvae (yellow arrows, Figure 4H,H').
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figures 4H and 4H'.

claim: The mutant ES appeared to completely lack openings in its apical junctions, as none were identified in mutants imaged by serial-section scanning EM or transmission EM.
source: Unlike the wild-type ES, however, the mutant ES appeared to completely lack openings in its apical junctions, as we were unable to identify any in mutants imaged by serial-section scanning EM or transmission EM (four total mutant ears).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM and transmission EM data from mutant samples.

claim: Long lamellar projections could not be found on the basal side of the mutant ES.
source: Consistent with the absence of thin protrusions in the sparsely labeled mutants (Figure 3J), we could not find long lamellar projections on the basal side of the mutant ES (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial-section EM data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Apical openings could not be identified in the wild-type ZO-1 immunostains.
source: We were unable to identify apical openings in the wild-type ZO-1 immunostains (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is a negative result from immunostaining experiments.

claim: The inability to identify apical openings in ZO-1 stains could be due to difficulty resolving small openings (~1 μm diameter) or to ZO-1 remaining present at the openings such that the apical barrier could reform after ES deflation to hold hydrostatic pressure.
source: This could be due to difficulty resolving small openings (~1 μm diameter) or to ZO-1 remaining present at the openings such that the apical barrier could reform after ES deflation to hold hydrostatic pressure.
evidence: This is speculation about why apical openings were not observed in ZO-1 stains.

claim: lmx1bb-dependent activity is necessary for openings to form in the apical junctions of ES tissue and for ES cells to extend thin basal protrusions.
source: These data suggest that lmx1bb-dependent activity is necessary for openings to form in the apical junctions of ES tissue and for ES cells to extend thin basal protrusions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type and mutant ES structures.

claim: The LLSM produced slightly blurred images with low signal-to-noise (SNR) without adaptive optics correction.
source: The LLSM produced slightly blurred images with low signal-to-noise (SNR, Figure 5B) without adaptive optics correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Adding the correction with an AO-LLSM system adequately compensated for tissue aberrations and produced images with higher SNR and better contrast.
source: Adding the correction with an AO-LLSM system adequately compensated for tissue aberrations and produced images with higher SNR and better contrast.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of images with and without AO shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Some cells stretched and thinned when the ES lumen was inflated and thickened upon deflation, likely a result of their elastic properties.
source: We found that some cells stretched and thinned when the ES lumen was inflated and thickened upon deflation, likely a result of their elastic properties (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and cell tracking shown in Figures 5H-I.

claim: There were instances when the cells at the tip of the ES did not thin during inflation, or while they thinned during some events, they did not thin during others.
source: However, there were instances when the cells at the tip of the ES did not thin during inflation, or while they thinned during some events, they did not thin during others (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and cell tracking shown in Figures 5J-K.

claim: For 43 of 99 tested trajectories, either cell thinning significantly correlated (p-value less than 10−3) with inflation or cell thickening significantly correlated with deflation.
source: For 43 of 99 tested trajectories, either cell thinning significantly correlated (p-value less than 10−3) with inflation or cell thickening significantly correlated with deflation (green region, Figure 5L, example of significantly correlated interval, bracket with green arrowhead, Figure 5H, same data point indicated with green arrowhead in Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claim: For 42 of 99 tested trajectories, cell behavior did not significantly correlate with inflation or deflation.
source: For 42 of 99 tested trajectories, cell behavior did not significantly correlate with inflation or deflation (grey region, Figure 5L, example of uncorrelated inflation interval, bracket with grey arrowhead, Figure 5J, same data point indicated with grey arrowhead in Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claim: For 14 of 99 tested trajectories there was significant correlation between inflation and cell thickening or deflation and cell thinning.
source: Unexpectedly, for 14 of 99 tested trajectories there was significant correlation between inflation and cell thickening or deflation and cell thinning (magenta region, Figure 5L, example of correlated interval, bracket with magenta arrowhead, Figure 5J, same data point indicated with magenta arrowhead in Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell thickness trajectories shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Stretching of a subset of cells contributes to regulation of increased pressure by allowing the ES lumen to expand.
source: While each cell's behavior is varied, these data suggest that stretching of a subset of cells contributes to regulation of increased pressure by allowing the ES lumen to expand.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell tracking and correlation analysis.

claim: Some cells appear to be pushed away from the ES lumen during inflation and pulled back into the ES epithelium during deflation.
source: Additionally, some cells appear to be pushed away from the ES lumen during inflation and pulled back into the ES epithelium during deflation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell tracking data showing unexpected correlations.

claim: The complexity of the response is likely the result of features we did not resolve such as the dynamics of each cell's basal lamellae, each cell's residual apical and lateral adhesion, and each cell's basal interface with the extracellular matrix.
source: The complexity of the response is likely the result of features we did not resolve such as the dynamics of each cell's basal lamellae, each cell's residual apical and lateral adhesion, and each cell's basal interface with the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of the complex cell behaviors observed.

claim: Some lamellae are rapidly extending and retracting like they are crawling over neighboring cells or neighboring lamellae.
source: 3D rendering of the AO-LLSM signal shows that some lamellae are rapidly extending and retracting like they are crawling over neighboring cells or neighboring lamellae (Video 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Video 11.

claim: Dynamic patches of increased intensity can shift rapidly in 3D renderings of the time course.
source: In 3D renderings of the time course we see dynamic patches of increased intensity that can shift rapidly (Figure 6A, Video 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6A and Video 11.

claim: Lamellae can crawl a few micrometers per minute.
source: By merging 3D renderings of 3 consecutive time points, 30 s apart, in red, blue, and then green, we observed the relative displacement of these lamellae that can crawl a few micrometers per minute (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data and analysis shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Inflations of the ES lumen coincided with slow increases in the surface area of exposed lamellae (30 min expansion).
source: Inflations of the ES lumen coincided with slow increases in the surface area of exposed lamellae (30 min expansion, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Some secondary loci included smaller lamellae that engaged and inflated much more quickly (1–2 min expansion).
source: Some secondary loci included smaller lamellae that engaged and inflated much more quickly (1–2 min expansion, Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The same locus can rapidly expand multiple times (one minute rapid expansions an hour apart).
source: This presentation reveals that the same locus can rapidly expand multiple times (one minute rapid expansions an hour apart, Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claim: Multiple sets of basal lamellae can simultaneously engage at different loci, either through slow spreading or rapid expansion.
source: In summary, multiple sets of basal lamellae can simultaneously engage at different loci, either through slow spreading or rapid expansion.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the AO-LLSM data showing different dynamics at different loci.

claim: Myosin localized to the apical domains of ES cells as well as to dynamic puncta at the basal membrane throughout both inflation and deflation of the ES.
source: Myosin localized to the apical domains of ES cells as well as to dynamic puncta at the basal membrane throughout both inflation and deflation of the ES.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of myosin-GFP shown in Figure 6H and Video 12.

claim: During ES inflation, contraction of apical myosin likely counteracts the stress of hydrostatic pressure and maintains the integrity of apical junctions.
source: During ES inflation, contraction of apical myosin likely counteracts the stress of hydrostatic pressure and maintains the integrity of apical junctions (Rauzi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed myosin localization and cited prior work on myosin function.

claim: Tension from apical myosin, strain from hydrostatic pressure, and the adhesion strength between junctional protein complexes likely determines the elastic limit of apical junctions.
source: Tension from apical myosin, strain from hydrostatic pressure, and the adhesion strength between junctional protein complexes likely determines the elastic limit of apical junctions.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanical factors determining apical junction behavior.

claim: The crossing of this elastic limit may cause the small apical openings observed in Figure 4G, which ultimately communicates the otic vesicle's hydrostatic pressure to the lamellar protrusions.
source: The crossing of this elastic limit may cause the small apical openings observed in Figure 4G, which ultimately communicates the otic vesicle's hydrostatic pressure to the lamellar protrusions.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of apical opening formation.

claim: The dynamic spots of basal myosin could indicate two possible activities: contraction to retract lamellar protrusions as observed during cell migration or contraction at focal adhesions.
source: The dynamic spots of basal myosin could indicate two possible activities: contraction to retract lamellar protrusions as observed during cell migration or contraction at focal adhesions.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of basal myosin puncta.

claim: Utrophin localized strongest at apical domains of ES cells.
source: Utrophin localized strongest at apical domains of ES cells (Figure 6H), but unfortunately bleached too quickly to generate any meaningful insights into the potential of actin localization dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of utrophin-mCherry shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Utrophin based actin highlighters do not localize to actin within lamellae.
source: It had been shown that utrophin based actin highlighters do not localize to actin within lamellae (Belin et al., 2014), which explains the relatively low amounts of basal utrophin signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Fluorescent phalloidin labels actin filament enrichment at both apical and basal domains of ES cells.
source: In contrast, fluorescent phalloidin labels actin filament enrichment at both apical and basal domains of ES cells (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Consistent apical localization of myosin throughout ES cycling suggests that the same contractility both counteracts hydrostatic pressure during inflation and drives deflation when hydrostatic pressure drops as the relief valve is opened.
source: Our observations of consistent apical localization of myosin throughout ES cycling suggests that the same contractility both counteracts hydrostatic pressure during inflation and drives deflation when hydrostatic pressure drops as the relief valve is opened.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed myosin localization patterns.

claim: No sudden changes in myosin localization or behavior were observed that would indicate regulation for either inflation or deflation.
source: We did not observe any sudden changes in myosin localization or behavior that would indicate regulation for either inflation or deflation.
evidence: This is a negative result from myosin imaging experiments.

claim: Analysis of myosin localization in lmx1bb crispants revealed similar apical localization and dynamic basal puncta.
source: Analysis of myosin localization in lmx1bb crispants (CRISPR-Cas9 knockout embryos) revealed similar apical localization and dynamic basal puncta (Figure 6I, Video 12, representative of 2 time-lapses).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of myosin-GFP in lmx1bb crispants shown in Figure 6I and Video 12.

claim: The distended ES rapidly collapsed after puncturing the otic vesicle with a tungsten needle (5/5 mutant puncture experiments caused ES collapse).
source: To determine whether the mutant ES tissue has elastic material properties, we punctured the otic vesicle with a tungsten needle and found that the distended ES rapidly collapsed (5/5 mutant puncture experiments caused ES collapse, Figure 6K).
evidence: This claim is supported by puncture experiments shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Global inhibition of actin or myosin with cytochalasin D or (S)-nitro-blebbistatin correlated with ES deflation.
source: Global inhibition of actin or myosin with cytochalasin D or (S)-nitro-blebbistatin correlated with ES deflation.
evidence: This claim is based on drug treatment experiments.

claim: It is currently impossible to determine whether ES deflation after global actin/myosin inhibition is owed to hydrostatic pressure not being maintained by the otic vesicle epithelium.
source: However, it is currently impossible to determine whether this is owed to hydrostatic pressure not being maintained by the otic vesicle epithelium.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the drug treatment results.

claim: Heat-shock induction of a dominant negative Rac1 at 56 hpf resulted in otic vesicles that became leaky and subsequently collapsed between 60 and 70 hpf (19/34 leaky and collapsed ears versus 1/12 in a heat-shock gfp control).
source: Heat-shock induction, throughout the embryo, of a dominant negative Rac1 at 56 hpf resulted in otic vesicles that became leaky and subsequently collapsed between 60 and 70 hpf (Video 13, 19/34 leaky and collapsed ears versus 1/12 in a heat-shock gfp control)(Kardash et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by heat-shock experiments shown in Video 13.

claim: Heat shock induction of the dominant negative Rac1 at 32 hpf, prior to ES formation, did not result in leaking or ear collapse during the subsequent 15 hr (0/20 leaky or collapsed ears versus 0/14 in a heat-shock gfp control).
source: In contrast, heat shock induction of the dominant negative Rac1 at 32 hpf, prior to ES formation, did not result in leaking or ear collapse during the subsequent 15 hr (while 0/20 leaky or collapsed ears versus and 0/14 in a heat-shock gfp control).
evidence: This claim is supported by heat-shock experiments at an earlier time point.

claim: These results are consistent with an important role for the basal lamellipodia of the ES for maintaining barrier integrity during inflation and deflation cycles.
source: These results are consistent with an important role for the basal lamellipodia of the ES for maintaining barrier integrity during inflation and deflation cycles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing-dependent effects of Rac1 inhibition.

claim: Instances were witnessed when membrane signal from inflated lamellae was disrupted prior to deflation.
source: We were able to witness instances when membrane signal from inflated lamellae was disrupted prior to deflation (yellow arrows, Figure 7A–D, lumen magenta, adjacent cells colored in at first at last time-points).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figures 7A-D.

claim: Breaks in membrane continuity preceded a deflation event (reduction in local volume of ES lumen).
source: Examination of the raw and rendered segmentations prior to and following breaks in membrane continuity showed that it preceded a deflation event (reduction in local volume of ES lumen, magenta, Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by AO-LLSM data shown in Figures 7A and 7C.

claim: Close examination of the path of endolymph release revealed a small opening through which endolymph travels out into the periotic space.
source: Close examination of the path of endolymph release revealed a small opening through which endolymph travels out into the periotic space (x-y and y-z planes at relief valve openings, yellow arrows, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by high temporal resolution imaging of labeled endolymph shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Narrow paths of pressure release were observed in all high time-resolution (20 s) time-lapse movies of endolymph dynamics (four fish in Video 14 exhibit 16 opening events).
source: Narrow paths of pressure release were observed in all high time-resolution (20 s) time-lapse movies of endolymph dynamics (four fish in Video 14 exhibit 16 opening events).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple time-lapse movies shown in Video 14.

claim: Pressure relief prevents endolymphatic hydrops—the buildup of pressure and potential tearing of the ear's epithelium—that is associated with many inner ear pathologies.
source: Primarily, pressure relief prevents endolymphatic hydrops—the buildup of pressure and potential tearing of the ear's epithelium—that is associated with many inner ear pathologies.
evidence: This is an inference about the primary function of the pressure relief valve based on the experimental findings.

claim: Low-frequency deflations of the ES may drive intermittent longitudinal flow of endolymph from the cochlea and semicircular canals into the endolymphatic duct and sac.
source: Secondarily, low-frequency deflations of the ES may drive intermittent longitudinal flow of endolymph from the cochlea and semicircular canals into the endolymphatic duct and sac.
evidence: This is speculation about a secondary function of the ES deflation cycles.

claim: The presence of longitudinal flow had been proposed to explain the accumulation of debris and tracers within the ES and, while never directly observed in an unperturbed inner ear, longitudinal flow can be induced and observed through manipulations of the inner ear.
source: The presence of longitudinal flow had been proposed to explain the accumulation of debris and tracers within the ES and, while never directly observed in an unperturbed inner ear, longitudinal flow can be induced and observed through manipulations of the inner ear (Salt, 2001; Salt and DeMott, 1998; Salt and Plontke, 2010; Salt et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on longitudinal flow.

claim: The localized inflation and patterned formation of valve cells leads to a localized break at the ES lamellar barriers.
source: The localized inflation and patterned formation of valve cells leads to a localized break at the ES lamellar barriers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed localized nature of ES inflation and valve structure.

claim: The local break could create a transient pressure gradient that leads to flow from other parts of the inner ear towards the endolymphatic duct and sac.
source: The local break could create a transient pressure gradient that leads to flow from other parts of the inner ear towards the endolymphatic duct and sac.
evidence: This is speculation about how localized breaks could drive longitudinal flow.

claim: The intermittent and slow nature of this flow could explain conflicting interpretations of classic studies using tracer injections where tracer accumulated in the ES after long periods of time but significant flow was absent when observed on short time scales.
source: The intermittent and slow nature of this flow could explain conflicting interpretations of classic studies using tracer injections where tracer accumulated in the ES after long periods of time but significant flow was absent when observed on short time scales (Guild, 1927; Manni and Kuijpers, 1987; Salt, 2001; Salt et al., 1986).
evidence: This is speculation about how the findings could reconcile prior conflicting observations, supported by citations.

claim: Longitudinal flow was observed in action with the expulsion of leaked-in perilymph.
source: We observed longitudinal flow in action with the expulsion of leaked-in perilymph (Figure 2G, Video 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2G and Video 5.

claim: Lmx1bb is a LIM homeobox transcription factor.
source: Lmx1bb is a LIM homeobox transcription factor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the identity of lmx1bb.

claim: Mutations in LMX1B cause Nail Patella syndrome in humans and a third of Nail Patella syndrome patients develop glaucoma, a phenotype also observed in mouse models.
source: Mutations in LMX1B cause Nail Patella syndrome in humans and a third of Nail Patella syndrome patients develop glaucoma, a phenotype also observed in mouse models (Cross et al., 2014; Liu and Johnson, 2010; Mimiwati et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Nail Patella syndrome.

claim: The mechanism by which glaucoma arises in the disease and in mouse models is not clear; however, the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal appear abnormal in these cases.
source: The mechanism by which glaucoma arises in the disease and in mouse models is not clear; however, the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal appear abnormal in these cases.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism while noting observed abnormalities.

claim: Giant vacuoles and pores in Schlemm's canal may be used to relieve intraocular pressure, and their ultrastructure resembles the lamellar barriers of the ES.
source: Giant vacuoles and pores in Schlemm's canal may be used to relieve intraocular pressure, and their ultrastructure resembles the lamellar barriers of the ES (Gong et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and includes an inference about structural similarity.

claim: Pulsatile pressure relief occurs in the eye, although at the higher frequency of the heart rate, and Schlemm's canal is a major site of the pressure relief.
source: Like the ear, pulsatile pressure relief occurs in the eye, although at the higher frequency of the heart rate, and Schlemm's canal is a major site of the pressure relief (Ascher, 1962; Johnstone et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ocular pressure relief.

claim: Up to half of Nail Patella syndrome patients suffer from kidney disease.
source: Additionally, up to half of Nail Patella syndrome patients suffer from kidney disease (Bennett et al., 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During podocyte maturation apical junctions are lost, thereby enabling development of the basal slit diaphragm that filters blood.
source: During podocyte maturation apical junctions are lost, thereby enabling development of the basal slit diaphragm that filters blood (Pavenstädt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on podocyte development.

claim: In mice lacking LMX1B activity, podocytes fail to lose their apical junctions.
source: In mice lacking LMX1B activity, podocytes fail to lose their apical junctions (Miner et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on LMX1B function in podocytes.

claim: Removal of apical junctions may be a specialized mechanism used in organs where elaborations of junction architectures allow controlled release of fluids from one compartment into another.
source: Removal of apical junctions may thus be a specialized mechanism used in organs where elaborations of junction architectures allow controlled release of fluids from one compartment into another.
evidence: This is speculation about a common mechanism across different organs based on the findings.

claim: The mouse Lmx1a mutant exhibits defects like the fish lmx1bb mutant in that they exhibit similarly enlarged ears.
source: Furthermore, the mouse Lmx1a mutant exhibits defects (Koo et al., 2009) like the fish lmx1bb mutant in that they exhibit similarly enlarged ears.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on mouse Lmx1a mutants.

claim: Similarity in its protein sequence and expression suggests that mouse Lmx1a and fish lmx1bb likely have comparable activities.
source: Similarity in its protein sequence and expression suggests that mouse Lmx1a and fish lmx1bb likely have comparable activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity and phenotypic similarity.

claim: LMX1 transcription factors may have a common set of targets in the ES, eye, and kidney involved in apical junction remodeling to regulate fluid flow across epithelia.
source: We speculate that LMX1 transcription factors may have a common set of targets in the ES, eye, and kidney involved in apical junction remodeling to regulate fluid flow across epithelia.
evidence: This is speculation about a common mechanism across different organs.

claim: Apical junctions and basal lamellae in the endolymphatic sac behave like a pressure relief valve to regulate fluctuating volume and pressure that arises from excess endolymph in the inner ear.
source: We find that apical junctions and basal lamellae in the endolymphatic sac behave like a pressure relief valve to regulate fluctuating volume and pressure that arises from excess endolymph in the inner ear (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: The high temporal and spatial resolution of AO-LLSM, combined with image processing tools for segmenting, tracking, and quantifying cell geometries, was necessary to reveal the dynamic cell behaviors underlying the pulsing of the ES.
source: The high temporal and spatial resolution of AO-LLSM, combined with image processing tools for segmenting, tracking, and quantifying cell geometries, was necessary to reveal the dynamic cell behaviors underlying the pulsing of the ES.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for the study.

claim: While cells of the ES are immobile epithelial cells, the cell extensions resemble lamellipodia of crawling cells in thickness (~40 nm), speed (as fast as ~1 μm per minute), and regulatory mechanism (Rac1).
source: While cells of the ES are immobile epithelial cells, the cell extensions resemble lamellipodia of crawling cells in thickness (40 nm), speed (as fast as ~1 μm per minute), and regulatory mechanism (Rac1) (Abercrombie, 1980).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the experimental findings and cited prior work.

claim: It remains unclear how each cell's basal lamellae, residual apical and lateral adhesion, and basal interface with the extracellular matrix contribute to the physical behavior of the ES.
source: Because of limitations of imaging, it remains unclear how each cell's basal lamellae, residual apical and lateral adhesion, and basal interface with the extracellular matrix contribute to the physical behavior of the ES.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in understanding the detailed mechanisms.

claim: The force of adhesion between crawling lamellae and their substrate, in combination with the viscoelastic properties of the ES, likely determines the relief valve's set point for volume and pressure homeostasis.
source: Of related interest is how the crawling lamellae adhere to their substrate in the ES to generate a barrier without gaps during the inflation phase. The force of this adhesion, in combination with the viscoelastic properties of the ES, likely determines the relief valve's set point for volume and pressure homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanical determinants of the valve's set point.

claim: For the inner ears of adult mammals, this set point is likely around 100–400 Pascals, although it is unknown how much the inner ear's pressure and volume fluctuate.
source: For the inner ears of adult mammals, this set point is likely around 100–400 Pascals, although it is unknown how much the inner ear's pressure and volume fluctuate (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on inner ear pressure.

claim: An instance of an incomplete deflation was observed in mutant over-inflation videos that contrasts with wild-type deflation cycles and mutant ES collapse after the otic vesicle was punctured.
source: In our mutant over-inflation videos we observed an instance of an incomplete deflation (Video 6) that contrasts with wild-type deflation cycles and mutant ES collapse after the otic vesicle was punctured (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Video 6 and Figure 6J.

claim: This difference raises the questions of how pathological tearing of otic epithelium from endolymphatic hydrops might lead to hearing and balance symptoms and whether the organization of the endolymphatic duct and sac prevents an influx of low potassium perilymph from coming into direct contact with the stereocilia of sensory hair cells.
source: This difference raises the questions of how pathological tearing of otic epithelium from endolymphatic hydrops might lead to hearing and balance symptoms and whether the organization of the endolymphatic duct and sac prevents an influx of low potassium perilymph from coming into direct contact with the stereocilia of sensory hair cells.
evidence: This identifies open questions raised by the findings.

claim: Determination of the molecular basis of lamellar barrier organization and apical junction dynamics will be necessary to make progress on how the physical relief valve works and how it might fail to cause disease.
source: Determination of the molecular basis of lamellar barrier organization and apical junction dynamics will be necessary to make progress on how the physical relief valve works and how it might fail to cause disease.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.
